sentences.text: Finn and Zeb go back in time to find out if dino mums stayed with their babies.
The sound of the story is ay, as in wait.
Tap a word to hear it.
Finn and Zeb are in the Den.
Did dino mums stay with their babies?
They put on the time packs and step into the Time Gate.
Up the hill to the cave.
The cave is dark and damp.
From the cave they can see a wide plain.
At the lake, the mud is deep and grey.
A line of dinos plods past.
Finn and Zeb trail them to the nests.
In one nest, ten tiny babies wait.
Each one is as long as a cat.
The babies peep and wave their tails.
But no mum can be seen.
A huge dino comes up the trail.
Her mouth is like a duck's bill.
She stays and drops plants in the nest.
One baby is out of the nest, in the rain.
Fossil hunters think Maiasaura mums looked after their babies for a long time.
So the mum would come back.
But a cold baby in the rain is hard to leave!
Real explorers do not all agree.
He lays it back in the nest.
Then the mum nudges it back.
They make a shelter from big leaves.
Finn makes a note: dino mums stay and bring food to the nest.
Zeb wants to see the babies play.
The gate hums and takes them home.
The babies play in the mud.
Back in the Den, Finn pins up the note.
Dino mums stayed with their babies and brought them food.
Finn and Zeb cracked the case!
The mums looked after their babies for a long time.
That is as long as a bus.
Fossil hunters found 14 nests in one spot.
The dinos nested together, like a big camp.
What did Finn and Zeb find in the mud?
What did the dino mum drop in the nest?
She brought plants for the babies to eat.
Why did Finn and Zeb go back in time?
To see if dino mums stay with their babies.
Nobody could say, so they went to see.
Why is good mother lizard a good name for Maiasaura?
The mum stays and brings food.
A good mum stays and brings food.
If you could go back in time, what would you want to see?
You earned the Dino Trail patch!
A giant fossil horn arrives at the Den.
Finn and Zeb go back in time to find out what the horns were for.
The sound of the story is or, as in horn.
A fossil horn has come in.
Time to go back and see.
They put on the time packs.
Then they hear a snort, and a stomp.
Big prints go north, and small prints go to the shore.
The big prints go past torn ferns.
Small prints lead to the shore.
A baby splashes, then trots off!
Finn and Zeb peek round a rock.
Two long horns stick out over its eyes, and a short one is on its nose.
It has a big bony frill and a beak like a parrot.
Then a second one stomps up.
They lower their horns and push.
It is a test of force.
Then one gets bored and trots off.
Finn makes a note: horns are for showing off, and for a push.
On the way back, Zeb spots an old horn tip in the mud.
Today, fossil hunters are asked to leave a special fossil where it is and get help from an expert, so it can be dug out with care.
But a horn from long ago could teach us so much!
Finn picks up the horn tip.
He wraps it up to take back to the Den.
They leave the horn tip in the mud.
One day it may turn into a fossil!
Finn draws the horn tip, every bump and crack.
Run for the gate, or shelter and wait?
They dash past the herd in the storm.
Under a ledge they wait for the storm to pass.
Then they stroll to the gate.
Back in the Den, Finn sorts his notes.
The horns were for showing off and for pushing contests.
Each long horn could be about 1 metre long, nearly as long as Finn is tall.
It had up to 160 teeth, about five times as many as a grown-up.
The big one with three horns and a frill.
How many horns did it have?
Two long ones and a short one on its nose.
Why did the two Triceratops push with their horns?
It was a test of force, not a fight.
Then one got bored and trotted off.
Why might a Triceratops need big horns and a frill?
To show off and to push.
If you had horns like a Triceratops, what would you use them for?
You earned the Three Horns patch!
Finn and Zeb fly to Mars to find a safe spot for the first space base.
The sound of the story is igh, as in night.
Finn and Zeb are in the Den at night.
Mars needs a safe spot for a space base.
The ship zooms high into the night sky.
Mars is a tiny red dot.
They land on wide, dry, red land.
Stop one: a cave in the side of a hill.
In the cave, a base can hide from the hot sun rays.
But it is dark all the time.
Stop two: the ice at the top of Mars.
Ice can melt into water to drink.
But at night it is colder than a freezer.
They hide behind a big rock.
Then the sky is pink again.
Finn must pick a spot for the base.
Space scientists have the same big question.
Some like caves and lava tubes, because the rock shields a base from the sun's rays.
Some like the ice, because ice means water.
The base will hide from the rays all day.
They will pile up thick white walls.
Not far from the ice, not far from the cave.
Finn sends the plan to Mars Control.
But Zeb wants to see the two tiny moons first.
They lift off into the pink sky.
Earth is a bright blue dot.
Two tiny moons shine in the sky.
Back in the Den that night, Finn pins up the plan.
Finn and Zeb found two good spots for a base on Mars and sent the plan home.
A day on Mars is about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth.
Mars has two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos.
Phobos is 26 km across, about a half-hour car trip.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the biggest volcano we know.
It is 27 km high, three times taller than Mount Everest.
A cave in the side of a hill.
What is at the top of Mars?
Why is the cave a good spot for a base?
It hides from the sun's rays.
The rock keeps the hot rays out.
Why would a base need the ice?
Ice is fun to slide on.
Would you rather live in the cave or by the ice?
You earned the Night Flight patch!
Something dark sits in the middle of our galaxy.
Finn and Zeb fly out to see a black hole, from a safe distance.
The sound of the story is ow, as in down.
Now there is a new case.
Finn counts down: three, two, one...
Past the Moon, past Mars, out and out.
The galaxy spins round and round.
Two ways: a bright cloud of new stars, or a dark, still way.
Inside the cloud, new stars glow like a crowd of torches.
Finn turns the lights down low.
Then they see it, far out in front.
A black hole, with a ring of light round it.
Its pull is so strong that not even light can get out.
A cloud of dust is spinning round and round it, faster and faster.
Their probe could zoom down for a closer look, but it could not come back.
Real scientists did not send anything there.
They joined up eight telescopes around the world to make one as big as the Earth, and took the first picture in 2022.
But a probe might find out new things too!
The probe zooms down, round and round.
They stay out here, safe and sound, and look with the big telescope.
The crew shout back: Stay out there, and look with care!
Finn takes a picture of the dark ring.
Now they know how it looks.
Fly the fast way, or the long way round, past the stars?
The ship shoots back down to Earth in a flash.
They loop round a planet with rings and wave to a comet.
Back in the Den, Finn pins up the picture of the ring.
They found the black hole in the middle of our galaxy and took its picture.
It is about 4 million times as heavy as our Sun.
It is so far away that its light takes 27,000 years to reach us.
Eight telescopes around the world worked together, like one telescope as big as the Earth.
Case File: The black hole in our galaxy.
Which picture shows the black hole?
A dark round spot with a ring of light.
What can you hear in space?
Why can nothing get out of a black hole?
Not even light can get out.
Why would a probe that goes down to the black hole not come back?
The pull would not let it get out.
It would get lost in the stars.
Nothing gets out, not even light.
Would you send the probe down?
You earned the Round and Round patch!
Finn and Zeb trek into the misty mountains to count a gorilla family.
The sound of the story is ee, as in deep.
A ranger needs them to count gorillas.
They fly to the misty green hills.
A jeep bumps up the steep, steep track.
Keep seven big steps back, says the ranger.
Finn sees a nest of leaves and a trail of bent plants.
The nest is a heap of leaves.
They creep along the trail of bent plants.
A big silverback sits in the green, eating leaves.
The silverback stands and beats his chest.
It means: this is my team.
The baby creeps up to Zeb.
It wants to see the camera!
Rangers say: step back, because gorillas can catch our germs.
But a baby that comes to you is hard to stop!
They keep as still as trees.
The baby peeks at Zeb, then sneezes!
They step back, step by step.
The baby squeaks, then bumps back to its mum.
Finn holds the camera up high.
Finn adds them to the count sheet.
They reach the jeep, wet but happy.
Back in the Den, the photos go up on the screen.
Four gorillas, safe and well, counted and photographed.
That is as heavy as two grown-ups.
A gorilla can eat 34 kg of plants in one day, about as heavy as Finn and Zeb together.
There are only about 1,000 mountain gorillas.
Rangers count them to keep them safe.
The big one with the silver back.
What did the silverback do with his chest?
Why did the ranger say to keep seven big steps back?
Our germs can make them ill.
Why does Finn count the gorillas?
Rangers count them so they know the family is safe and well.
Would you keep still or step back if the baby came to you?
You earned the Deep Green patch!
Which bird is the fastest on Earth?
Finn and Zeb climb a church tower in the city to find out.
The sound of the story is ur, as in bird.
A ranger sends a clue: a bird that nests on a church in the city.
They get to the church first thing.
Its tower is as tall as ten houses!
The ranger sets up a big telescope.
A bird on the third ledge up.
It has a dark head, like a helmet, and a pale chest.
Do they go up the tower stairs, or stay and watch from the church yard?
Up they go, step after step.
They burst out at the top, puffing.
They sit on a bench in the church yard.
Zeb spots a feather twirling down.
Then she tips over and dives!
She curls her wings in, like a dart.
She is faster than a car on a motorway.
No bird on Earth can dive faster!
She misses, and turns back up.
She lands back on her ledge.
Three fluffy chicks peep out of the nest.
The church wants a camera on the nest so people can watch.
Lots of cathedrals do put cameras by falcon nests, so people all over can watch the chicks grow.
Others say: give the birds peace, and watch from far away with a telescope.
By law, nobody may disturb a falcon nest.
A small camera goes up by the nest.
Now people all over can see the birds!
They leave the birds in peace.
The chicks curl up and snooze.
They watch from far with the telescope.
Zeb sees the first chick flap its wings!
Finn writes in his notebook: fastest bird on Earth, nests on churches.
Get the train home first, or stay to see her last flight?
On the train, Zeb curls up and snores.
She swirls up high, then turns and dives one last time, a dark dart in the sky.
Back in the Den, Finn pins up the bird.
The peregrine falcon is the fastest bird on Earth.
A peregrine can dive at 320 km an hour.
That is about three times as fast as a car on a motorway.
Now some nest on tall buildings in towns, like cathedrals.
In 1961 there were only 385 pairs in the UK.
Which picture shows the falcon diving?
Wings curled in, like a dart.
On a ledge, high up on the church.
Why did she curl her wings in when she dived?
To go faster, like a dart.
Why do people keep away from a falcon nest?
So the birds are not upset.
Because falcons do not like chips.
The birds need peace to look after their chicks.
Would you put a camera on the nest?
You earned the Fastest Bird patch!
With Finn's Shrink Torch, he goes down into a real rabbit burrow!
The sound of the story is air, as in hair.
Zeb's best case yet: a pair of rabbits!
A grassy hill is full of holes.
Rabbits live there, in tunnels under the hill.
Where should they sit and watch?
On the hill, or by the hedge?
On the hill they keep still and stare.
A rabbit hops right past Zeb's feet!
By the hedge they spot a hare!
It is bigger, with long legs.
Zeb wants to see down there.
Finn has a gadget to spare: the Shrink Torch!
It is dark, but he is not scared!
It hops off, and Zeb follows it.
In a snug nest of grass and fur, baby rabbits sleep.
Up the stairs of earth Zeb climbs, into the fresh air.
The rabbits nibble the farm crops.
Farmers and rabbit fans do not always agree.
Some farmers put up rabbit-proof fences to keep their crops safe.
Some farms leave wild strips at the edges of fields for animals.
People still talk about the best way.
The rabbits stare, then hop to the hill.
They let the rabbits share the field.
They plant a patch of clover just for the rabbits.
Go home now, or wait for the rabbits to come out and play?
They wave to the farmer and head home in the fresh air.
At dusk, lots of rabbits pop up!
Back in the Den, Zeb draws a pair of rabbits.
Rabbits live in burrows under the ground, and Zeb went down one!
Up to 30 rabbits can share one warren, a home of tunnels and rooms under the ground.
They are born blind, and their eyes open when they are about 10 days old.
A rabbit's teeth never stop growing, so it chews and chews to keep them short.
Which picture shows Zeb in the burrow?
Down the tunnel, with his head torch on.
Why did Finn hold a string?
So Zeb could find his way back up.
The string led Zeb back up the tunnel.
Why was the farmer cross with the rabbits?
Rabbits eat the plants the farmer grows.
If you could shrink like Zeb, which animal's home would you go into?
You earned the Down the Burrow patch!
Finn and Zeb dive into the dark sea to find out what is glowing below the boat.
The sound of the story is oa, as in boat.
A boat crew saw a glow in the sea at night.
They load the boat and float out to sea.
a soft blue glow below the boat!
Zeb zips up his dive suit.
Zeb gives a thumbs up: OK!
The glow goes two ways: along the rocks, or down the slope.
Along the rocks, a crab blows bubbles.
A moray pokes its nose out.
Down the slope it is dark and cold.
Zeb's torch shows a stone dome.
They flash blue as they float past.
It can hide in a tiny hole.
It goes pink, then brown, then white!
An octopus can change its coat to hide.
The octopus grabs Zeb's torch with one arm!
Divers say octopuses are clever and curious, and they like to grab new things.
Most let go in the end.
But would you wait, or swap?
It drops it and slides away.
Finn slowly holds out a shell.
The octopus takes it and lets the torch go.
The octopus gets bored and slides back into its hole.
A turtle glides past, slow and calm.
It goes up for a breath, then back to doze.
Up the rope, or ride the pod?
Zeb goes up the rope, hand over hand.
Up they float, past the glow, up to the moonlit boat.
On the boat, Finn writes: the glow is tiny jellyfish!
The glow was hundreds of tiny jellyfish, and an octopus nearly kept Zeb's torch!
An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
Eight arms makes about 1,600 suckers, more than all the children in a big school.
A big one is 4 metres from arm tip to arm tip, as long as a car.
Hundreds of tiny jellyfish, flashing blue.
What colours did the octopus go?
It changes its coat to hide.
Why did the turtle go up to the top?
Why can an octopus hide in a tiny hole?
No bones, so it can squeeze into tiny gaps.
What would you swap with the octopus to get the torch back?
You earned the Glow Below patch!
A boat crew hears a deep, low tune in the sea.
Finn and Zeb sail out to find the singer.
The sound of the story is oo, as in blue.
A new case: a deep tune in the sea.
A boat crew drops a mic into the sea.
They hear a huge, low tune.
The crew picks up Finn and Zeb.
A few birds dive to the east.
The tune comes from the deep.
The birds dive into a pink patch of krill.
A huge crowd of tiny shrimps!
They follow the tune out to the deep blue.
A huge spout of spray, as tall as a house.
It is huge, longer than two buses!
The biggest animal there has ever been.
It opens its huge mouth and gulps up the krill.
Then it spits out the water.
A calf swims up to the boat!
Other boats would love to see the whales.
Whale watching helps people love whales and want to keep them safe.
But lots of boats can upset them.
So good crews go slowly, keep far back, never chase, and do not stay too long.
They come slowly, and lots of people see the huge blue.
Just the crew, the whales and the blue sea.
It comes slowly and keeps far back.
The whale sings its tune once more.
It can be heard far, far across the sea.
Zeb wants to see one last spout.
A last spout, and the huge tail lifts up.
The crew see the spout far off.
Back in the Den, Finn plays the tune.
The deep tune was a blue whale singing.
A blue whale can be up to 30 metres long.
That is as long as three buses.
The biggest blue whales can eat up to 6 tonnes of krill in a day.
That is as heavy as a big elephant.
Other whales can hear a blue whale's call 1,600 km away.
That is further than from London to Rome!
Which picture shows the whale's spout?
What does a blue whale eat?
Tiny shrimps called krill, lots and lots of them.
Why did Finn turn the motor off?
So the calf was safe and calm.
A quiet boat keeps whales calm.
Why could the crew hear the whale from far away?
Its deep tune goes far in the sea.
The whale was by the boat.
Whale tunes can be heard far, far across the sea.
Would you tell the other boats about the whales?
You earned the Huge Blue patch!
Finn and Zeb trek across Nepal to climb Mount Everest, then make a big jump on the way home.
The sound of the story is ar, as in far.
The case: climb the highest peak.
They fly far, far away to Nepal.
He is a Sherpa and knows the way.
They march up and down hills, past yaks and prayer flags.
Each day the path gets steep and hard.
At night the stars are so bright!
Cross the swing bridge, or go the long way round?
The bridge sways far above the river.
Down in the valley, a yak and her calf graze by a farm.
At Base Camp the tents are bright dots.
Zeb puts on a thick scarf.
Up they go, clipped to a rope.
Sharp spikes on their boots grip the ice.
Halfway up, the air is thin.
They put on masks to help.
Near the top, a dark cloud rolls in.
Wait for the wind to drop.
Real climbers pick a turn-back time before they set off.
If they are not at the top by then, they go back down, because getting down safely matters just as much.
Some wait for better weather, and some come back another year.
They keep going, step by step, slow and hard.
They sit in a hollow and wait.
Then the dark cloud drifts off.
They can see far over the peaks.
On the way down, they hear a roar.
It crashes into a dark gorge.
Stand in the spray, or watch from far back?
From far back they see a rainbow arch over the gorge.
Zeb is a star at hopping.
A gorge, too far to step!
Pasang clips them to a rope.
They sail over the gorge and land on the far side.
Back in the Den, Finn pins up a photo of the top.
Finn and Zeb climbed to the top of the world, and made it safely home.
That is about six and a half Ben Nevises stacked up!
Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa, and Edmund Hillary were the first people to reach the top, in 1953.
At the top, each breath has only about a third of the oxygen you get at the seaside.
That is why most climbers use oxygen masks.
Which picture shows the top of Everest?
Finn planted a flag on the top of the world.
Who led the way up the mountain?
Why did they put on masks halfway up?
The air is thin up high.
High up there is less air to breathe.
Why did Pasang clip them to a rope before the jump?
To pull them up a hill.
A rope keeps you safe if you slip.
Would you go on to the top, or wait for the wind to drop?
You earned the Top of the World patch!
